messages.text: Is a customer deposit revenue? My friend Chris says his catering company counts it as a sale the day it lands.

blocks.md:
Short answer: no, and Chris’s books are flattering him. A deposit is cash he’s holding for work he still owes. Until the event happens, it’s a **liability** (unearned revenue), not a sale.

If he books it as revenue on day one, a busy booking month looks hugely profitable even if every event is still ahead of him, and a cancellation leaves a hole.

suggestions: What if the event gets cancelled?

messages.text: Can you go back to normal? The blunt style is a bit much this early. And show me how a deposit actually moves through the books.

blocks.md: Back to balanced from here on. Here’s the path a deposit takes, using Emily’s catering example from Monday:

visual.title: A $4,000 catering deposit, from bank to books

steps.label: Deposit lands
steps.detail: Cash +$4,000; a $4,000 liability: she owes the event

steps.label: Ingredients bought
steps.detail: Cash −$2,500, held as a cost of the event

visual.takeaway: The cash arrives first; the revenue only exists once the work is done.

blocks.md: The same shape shows up on an income statement: revenue appears only in the month of the event. Wednesday’s session on reading an income statement builds on exactly this, and it’s still open if you want to finish it.
